newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy extends car buying incentive scheme.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy extends car buying incentive scheme.

text.p: Italy's cabinet agreed on Wednesday to extend the nation's car buying incentive scheme for a further 10 months, but it scaled back payments and moved to encourage the buying of more environmentally friendly cars.

Italy introduced its original scheme at the beginning of the year to run to end-September whereby owners of cars of over 10 years old could trade them in for scrapping in exchange for price discounts on new car purchases.

Industry minister PierLuigi Bersani announced the scheme extension to end-July 1998 after a cabinet meeting, and added that the extra cost of funding the scheme would be more than met by extra revenue from car taxes.
Bersani said that the scheme, "had positive impacts on the environment, the recovery of car production and also helped support GDP".

Under the current programme running from January to September, the government offers motorists a price discount of between 1.5 million ($838) and two million lire depending on engine size, a sum that is matched by the car manufacturers.

The new bill sets out that in the period October 1 1997 to January 31 1998, the cash incentive for car owners to trade in their old cars for new ones will be 1.5 million lire, again planned to be matched by the car industry.

While from February 1 to July 31 1998, the incentives will be structured to be "ecofriendly" and give larger amounts to cars which use less fuel. For cars that consume between seven and nine litres per 100 km the incentive will be 1.25 million lire and for those less than seven litres/100 km it will be 1.5 million.

Also from July 31 1998, there will be a total cash incentive from government and industry of four million lire for trading in an old car for a new electric-powered one and two million lire for one that runs on methane gas.
Bersani said that if parliament does not approve the bill by September, then the government will make it law by decree.

The incentive scheme has had a positive effect on the Italian car market with latest figures showing June new car registrations up 50.7 percent to 222,800, and new registrations for the first half of 1997 up 31.3 percent to 1.31 million.
The extension of Italy's car incentive scheme, will cost around 153 billion lire, but this will be more than covered by increased revenues, said Bersani.
"We calculate that the net revenue from the scheme for the whole of 1997 from vehicles sold will be more than 800 billion lire," he told a news conference.

In early June, car research body Centro Studi Promotor (CSP) said the scheme had cost the government some 574 billion lire in the first five months but added that income from VAT and new car registration tax brought to the state 1.051 trillion lire, giving the Italian government a net benefit of 477 billion lire.

But some analysts pointed out that although the scheme helped the consumers and helped the government it does penalise the manufacturers, and a similar scheme in France initially pushed up sales, only for them to collapse later.
"Schemes like this did not help the French, do nothing for margins and I can only see the bump at the end of the scheme being that much greater," said one industry analyst.

The extension was largely expected and although it did favour Italian car giant Fiat with its bias towards smaller cars, Fiat shares ended the day off 0.08 percent at 6,045 lire in a firmer Milan stock market.
